course.title: JavaScript Canvas Game Development Mastery
course.description: A comprehensive 40-part course taking you from absolute beginner to confident game developer using HTML5 Canvas and JavaScript. Covers Canvas API fundamentals, game loops, physics, animation, collision detection, sprite systems, particle effects, sound, AI, and complete architectural design of 4 full games: Pong, Flappy Bird, Platformer, and Space Shooter.

blocks.value: Welcome to Canvas Game Development

HTML5 Canvas is a powerful drawing API that lets you render graphics, animations, and entire games directly in the browser using JavaScript. Unlike DOM-based games, Canvas gives you pixel-level control over every frame — making it the industry standard for 2D web games.

blocks.alt: Diagram showing browser window with Canvas element rendering game graphics via JavaScript
blocks.caption: Canvas acts as a blank slate that JavaScript paints onto every frame

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Infographic/Diagram — A browser window showing a Canvas element in the center. Arrows show: JavaScript code → Canvas 2D Context → Rendered graphics (shapes, sprites, text). Include browser UI (URL bar, tabs) to ground it in reality. Use modern flat design with Canvas blue (#E44D26) and JS yellow (#F7DF1E) colors.
Why Canvas for Games?

• **Pixel-perfect control** — draw anything, not limited by HTML/CSS
• **60 FPS rendering** — hardware-accelerated 2D graphics
• **No DOM overhead** — thousands of sprites without lag
• **Cross-platform** — works on desktop, mobile, and tablets
• **Industry standard** — used by Phaser, PixiJS, and major game engines

blocks.alt: Comparison showing DOM-based game lagging vs Canvas game running smoothly with many sprites
blocks.caption: Canvas handles thousands of moving objects where the DOM struggles

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Split Comparison — Left: DOM game with 100 div elements, choppy FPS counter in red (15 FPS). Right: Canvas game with 1000 particles, smooth FPS counter in green (60 FPS). Use performance graphs or simple visual metaphors. Label 'DOM Limitations' vs 'Canvas Power'.
The Rendering Pipeline

Every Canvas game follows a loop: Clear the canvas → Update game state → Draw everything → Repeat. This happens 60 times per second. The browser calls your draw function via requestAnimationFrame() for smooth, synchronized rendering.

blocks.output: A blue rectangle with white text 'Hello, Canvas!' rendered on the canvas

blocks.question: What is the primary purpose of HTML5 Canvas?
options: To style web pages with CSS
To draw graphics and animations via JavaScript
blocks.correctAnswer: To draw graphics and animations via JavaScript
blocks.explanation: Canvas is a drawing surface controlled entirely by JavaScript. It has no styling capabilities of its own — everything is rendered programmatically.

blocks.question: Which method gets the drawing context for 2D graphics?
blocks.explanation: getContext('2d') returns the CanvasRenderingContext2D object, which provides all drawing methods like fillRect, strokeRect, and arc.

blocks.question: What HTML tag is used to create a canvas element?
blocks.explanation: The <canvas> tag creates the drawing surface in HTML. You must then use JavaScript to actually draw on it.

parts.partTitle: Part 2: Setting Up Your Development Environment

blocks.value: Your Game Dev Workspace

Before building games, you need a solid development environment. We'll use VS Code (free, fast, excellent JavaScript support), a local server (for module imports), and browser DevTools for debugging. No frameworks yet — pure Canvas and vanilla JS.

blocks.alt: VS Code editor showing Canvas game project with Live Server extension running
blocks.caption: VS Code with Live Server is the recommended setup for Canvas development

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Screenshot — VS Code window showing a project with index.html, game.js, and styles.css files in the sidebar. The editor shows a Canvas setup. The bottom status bar shows 'Live Server: Port 5500'. Dark theme preferred. Include the Live Server extension icon highlighted.
Project Structure

Organize your game project from day one. A clean folder structure prevents chaos as your game grows:

📁 my-canvas-game/
├── 📄 index.html
├── 📄 styles.css
├── 📁 js/
│   ├── 📄 main.js
│   ├── 📄 game.js
│   └── 📄 utils.js
└── 📁 assets/
    ├── 📁 images/
    ├── 📁 audio/
    └── 📁 fonts/

blocks.alt: File explorer showing organized game project folder structure
blocks.caption: A well-organized project scales from prototype to production

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: File Tree Diagram — Clean tree structure showing folders and files. Use folder icons (yellow) and file icons (white with extensions). Color-code by type: HTML (orange), CSS (blue), JS (yellow), assets (green). Include a small note: 'Start simple, grow organized'.

<!-- index.html -- Your game's entry point -->
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
    <title>My Canvas Game</title>
    <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">
</head>
<body>
    <!-- The canvas where magic happens -->
    <canvas id="gameCanvas"></canvas>
    
    <!-- Load game logic -->
    <script type="module" src="js/main.js"></script>
</body>
</html>
blocks.output: A blank HTML page with a canvas element ready for drawing

blocks.value: CSS for Full-Screen Canvas
Use CSS to make your canvas fill the screen and remove default margins. The canvas will maintain its internal resolution while stretching to fit the window.

blocks.output: Full-screen centered canvas with dark background and subtle border

blocks.value: JavaScript Module Setup
Using ES6 modules (type="module") keeps your code organized. Each file handles one responsibility: main.js bootstraps, game.js runs the loop, utils.js holds helpers.

blocks.output: Game instance created and started when page loads
A red square animating smoothly at 60 FPS on a dark background

blocks.question: Why do we use type="module" in the script tag?
options: To make the code run faster
blocks.explanation: type="module" tells the browser to treat the script as an ES6 module, allowing import/export statements for clean code organization.

blocks.question: What CSS property prevents scrollbars when canvas is full-screen?
blocks.explanation: overflow: hidden on the body element prevents scrollbars from appearing when the canvas fills the viewport.

blocks.question: Which HTML attribute on <script> enables ES6 module imports?
blocks.explanation: The type="module" attribute is required to use import/export syntax in browser JavaScript without a bundler.

parts.partTitle: Part 3: The Canvas 2D Context — Drawing Primitives

blocks.value: Drawing Shapes and Paths

The Canvas 2D Context (ctx) is your paintbrush. It provides methods to draw rectangles, circles, lines, curves, and text. Master these primitives — they are the building blocks of every game object you'll ever create.

blocks.alt: Canvas showing various shapes: filled rect, stroked circle, line path, arc, and text
blocks.caption: Canvas primitives: rectangles, circles, lines, arcs, and text

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Reference Sheet — A canvas with labeled examples: 'fillRect' (blue filled rectangle), 'strokeRect' (red outlined rectangle), 'arc' (green circle), 'lineTo' (purple zigzag path), 'fillText' (orange text). Each with a small arrow and label. Clean, educational style with a grid background.
Rectangles and Colors
The simplest shapes to draw. fillRect() draws a solid rectangle; strokeRect() draws just the outline. Set colors using fillStyle and strokeStyle before drawing.

blocks.output: A red filled rectangle, a blue outlined rectangle, and a transparent rectangle cutout

blocks.value: Circles and Arcs
Use arc() for circles and arcs. The angles are in radians, not degrees. Math.PI = 180°, so a full circle is Math.PI * 2.

blocks.output: A full orange circle and a yellow pac-man shape

blocks.value: Paths and Lines
For custom shapes, use paths: beginPath() starts a new shape, moveTo() positions the pen, lineTo() draws lines, and closePath() connects back to the start.

blocks.output: A purple triangle and a golden star drawn with path commands

blocks.value: Text Rendering
Display scores, health bars, and UI text. Use fillText() for solid text and strokeText() for outlined text. The font property accepts CSS font syntax.

blocks.output: White 'Score: 1000' text and red outlined 'GAME OVER' text on canvas

blocks.value: State Stack: Save and Restore
Canvas drawing state (colors, transforms, clipping) can be saved and restored. This is crucial for nested drawing operations and preventing style leaks.

blocks.output: Two rectangles: one translated to (100,100) in red, one at (0,0) in default black

blocks.question: What unit does Canvas use for angles in arc()?
blocks.explanation: Canvas uses radians for all angle measurements. Math.PI is 180°, so a full circle is Math.PI * 2.

blocks.question: Which method starts a new path for drawing custom shapes?
blocks.explanation: beginPath() clears the current path and starts a new one. Without it, new lines connect to the previous path's end point.

blocks.question: Which property sets the color used by fillRect() and fill()?
blocks.explanation: fillStyle sets the color, gradient, or pattern used for filling shapes. It must be set BEFORE calling fill() or fillRect().

parts.partTitle: Part 4: The Game Loop and Delta Time

blocks.value: The Heartbeat of Every Game

The game loop is the most important concept in game development. It runs continuously, updating game state and rendering frames. A well-designed loop runs at 60 FPS (frames per second) and remains smooth even when the browser is busy.

blocks.alt: Circular diagram showing game loop: Process Input → Update → Draw → Repeat
blocks.caption: The game loop: process input, update state, render frame, repeat forever

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Circular Flowchart — A large circle divided into three segments with arrows: 1) 'Process Input' (keyboard/mouse icon, blue), 2) 'Update State' (gear icon, green), 3) 'Render Frame' (monitor icon, red). Arrows flow clockwise with '60x/second' label. Center shows a clock face. Clean, modern design.
requestAnimationFrame
Never use setInterval for games! requestAnimationFrame() syncs with the monitor's refresh rate, pauses in background tabs (saving battery), and provides a timestamp for calculating delta time.

blocks.output: Smooth 60 FPS game loop running continuously

blocks.value: Delta Time: Frame-Independent Movement
Without delta time, your game runs at different speeds on different computers. Multiply all movement by deltaTime so objects move at consistent speeds regardless of frame rate.

blocks.alt: Comparison showing object moving same distance in 1 second at 30 FPS vs 60 FPS using delta time
blocks.caption: Delta time ensures consistent speed across all frame rates

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Comparison Diagram — Top timeline: 30 FPS (frames spaced far apart). Bottom timeline: 60 FPS (frames close together). Both show a ball moving from left to right, ending at the same position after 1 second. Label 'Without dt: Ball moves slower at 30 FPS' (red X) vs 'With dt: Same speed at any FPS' (green check). Use distance markers.

blocks.output: Player moves at exactly 200 pixels/second on any monitor

blocks.value: FPS Counter
Monitor your game's performance with a real-time FPS counter. If FPS drops below 60, you know your update or draw functions are too heavy.

blocks.output: Green 'FPS: 60' text displayed in the top-left corner of canvas

blocks.value: Fixed Time Steps for Physics
For stable physics (collision detection, velocity calculations), use a fixed time step. Update physics at a constant rate (e.g., 60Hz) while rendering as fast as possible.

blocks.output: Physics simulation running at fixed 60Hz with smooth variable-FPS rendering

blocks.question: Why should you use requestAnimationFrame instead of setInterval?
options: It syncs with monitor refresh and saves battery
blocks.correctAnswer: It syncs with monitor refresh and saves battery
blocks.explanation: requestAnimationFrame matches the monitor's refresh rate, pauses in background tabs, and provides timestamps for delta time calculations.

blocks.question: What does delta time (dt) represent?
options: The total game time in seconds
Time elapsed since the last frame in seconds
The number of frames per second
blocks.correctAnswer: Time elapsed since the last frame in seconds
blocks.explanation: Delta time is the duration between the current frame and the previous frame, measured in seconds. It makes movement frame-rate independent.

blocks.question: Which method schedules the next frame and provides a timestamp?
blocks.explanation: requestAnimationFrame(callback) schedules the browser to call your function before the next repaint, passing a high-resolution timestamp.

parts.partTitle: Part 5: Keyboard and Mouse Input Handling

blocks.value: Capturing Player Input

Games are interactive. You need to detect when players press keys, move the mouse, or click. Canvas doesn't have built-in input — you listen to browser events and track the state yourself. A clean input manager is essential for responsive controls.

blocks.alt: Diagram showing keyboard and mouse events flowing into an Input Manager that updates game state
blocks.caption: Input events flow through a manager that tracks current key and mouse states

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Flow Diagram — Left side: Keyboard (key icon) and Mouse (cursor icon) sending events. Center: 'InputManager' box with internal state maps (keysDown, mousePos). Right: Game objects reading from InputManager. Arrows show event flow. Use blue for keyboard, orange for mouse, green for manager.
Keyboard State Tracking
Don't check events inside your game loop! Instead, maintain a state object that tracks which keys are currently pressed. Check this state during update().

blocks.output: Responsive keyboard controls with support for held keys and single-press actions

blocks.value: Mouse Position and Clicks
Get mouse coordinates relative to the canvas (not the window). Handle clicks, movement, and button states for aiming, shooting, and UI interaction.

blocks.output: Mouse tracking relative to canvas with click detection

blocks.value: Touch Input for Mobile
Mobile games use touch events. Map touchstart, touchmove, and touchend to your input system. Prevent default to stop page scrolling.

blocks.output: Multi-touch input support for mobile devices

blocks.value: Common Key Codes Reference
Modern JavaScript uses e.code (physical key) instead of e.keyCode (deprecated). Here are the most common game controls:

blocks.output: Clean, maintainable control mapping using e.code values

blocks.value: Input Buffering
Input buffering stores recent inputs for a short time. This makes controls feel responsive — e.g., pressing jump 50ms before landing still registers.

blocks.output: Jump input buffered for 100ms, making controls feel more forgiving

blocks.question: Why track key states instead of handling events directly in the game loop?
options: Events are unpredictable; state polling is reliable
blocks.correctAnswer: Events are unpredictable; state polling is reliable
blocks.explanation: Events fire asynchronously. By storing key states, you can check them predictably during your update() function every frame.

blocks.question: Which property gives the physical key location regardless of keyboard layout?
blocks.explanation: e.code returns the physical key location (e.g., 'KeyW', 'ArrowLeft'), making controls consistent across different keyboard layouts and languages.

blocks.question: Which event prevents default touch scrolling on mobile?
blocks.explanation: Calling e.preventDefault() in touch event handlers stops the browser from scrolling the page, keeping the game in control.

blocks.value: Mastering Canvas Transforms

Canvas transforms let you translate (move), rotate, and scale the drawing context. Instead of calculating every vertex manually, you transform the coordinate system and draw as if nothing moved. This is essential for rotating sprites, scaling UI, and creating camera systems.

blocks.alt: Diagram showing original coordinate system vs translated, rotated, and scaled versions with a rectangle drawn in each
blocks.caption: Transforms modify the coordinate system, not the shapes themselves

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Four-panel Diagram — Panel 1: 'Original' — rectangle at (0,0). Panel 2: 'translate(100, 50)' — same rectangle drawn at offset position. Panel 3: 'rotate(45°)' — rectangle tilted. Panel 4: 'scale(2, 0.5)' — rectangle stretched. Each panel shows the transformed grid lines. Use different colors per transform type.
Translate, Rotate, Scale
The three fundamental transforms. Order matters: translate then rotate produces different results than rotate then translate. Always use save() and restore() to isolate transforms.

blocks.output: A red diamond (rotated square) and a blue stretched rectangle

blocks.value: The Transform Matrix
Under the hood, Canvas maintains a 3×3 transformation matrix. You can set it directly with setTransform() for absolute control — useful for camera systems and complex hierarchies.

blocks.output: Rectangle transformed by a custom matrix combining scale, rotation, and translation

blocks.value: Camera System: World vs Screen Space

Games have world coordinates (where objects exist) and screen coordinates (where they're drawn). A camera transform converts between them. Move the camera by translating the context in the opposite direction.

blocks.alt: Diagram showing world space with player at (1000, 500) and camera viewport centered on player, mapped to screen coordinates
blocks.caption: The camera transform converts world coordinates to screen coordinates

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Diagram — Left: 'World Space' — large grid with player at (1000, 500), camera box around player. Right: 'Screen Space' — same camera content filling the canvas. Arrow labeled 'Camera Transform' between them. Show the math: screenX = worldX - cameraX + canvasWidth/2. Use coordinate axes with different colors.

blocks.output: Camera follows player, rendering world objects in correct screen positions

blocks.value: Parallax Scrolling
Create depth by moving background layers at different speeds. Far layers move slower than near layers, simulating 3D perspective on a 2D canvas.

blocks.output: Smooth parallax scrolling with three depth layers

blocks.question: What happens if you call rotate() before translate()?
options: Same result as translate then rotate
The rotation happens around the original origin, then translation moves the rotated object
blocks.correctAnswer: The rotation happens around the original origin, then translation moves the rotated object
blocks.explanation: Transform order matters! rotate() then translate() rotates first (around 0,0), then moves. translate() then rotate() moves first, then rotates around the new origin.

blocks.question: Which method isolates transforms so they don't affect subsequent drawings?
blocks.explanation: save() pushes the current state (transforms, styles, clipping) onto a stack. restore() pops it back, undoing any changes made between them.

blocks.question: Which transform method moves the coordinate origin to a new position?
blocks.explanation: translate(x, y) moves the canvas origin to the specified coordinates. All subsequent drawings are relative to this new origin.

blocks.value: Bringing Games to Life

Animation is the illusion of movement created by rapidly displaying slightly different images. In Canvas games, you animate by updating object properties (position, rotation, scale) each frame and redrawing. Master easing, tweening, and sprite animation to make your games feel polished.

blocks.alt: Sequence showing a ball bouncing with position updates each frame, creating smooth animation
blocks.caption: Animation = updating properties + redrawing every frame

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Frame Sequence — 6 frames in a row showing a red ball at different heights: high, medium, low, bounce, medium, high. Arrows between frames labeled '16ms' (60 FPS). Below: code snippet showing y += vy; vy += gravity; draw(). Use motion blur effect on falling frames.
Linear Interpolation (Lerp)
Lerp smoothly transitions between two values. It's the foundation of all smooth animation — UI sliding, camera following, color fading, and more.

blocks.output: Camera smoothly follows player; health bar animates damage visually

blocks.value: Easing Functions

Easing makes animation feel natural. Linear movement looks robotic; easing adds acceleration and deceleration. Common easings: easeIn (start slow), easeOut (end slow), easeInOut (both), and elastic/bounce for playful effects.

blocks.alt: Graphs showing linear, easeIn, easeOut, easeInOut, and bounce easing curves
blocks.caption: Different easing curves produce different animation feels

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Graph Collection — Five small graphs side by side, each showing x-axis 'time' and y-axis 'value'. 1) Linear: straight diagonal. 2) easeIn: curve starting flat, getting steeper. 3) easeOut: curve starting steep, flattening. 4) easeInOut: S-curve. 5) bounce: curve with overshoot bounces. Color-code each curve differently.

blocks.output: Button bounces into view with realistic physics-like easing

blocks.value: Sprite Sheet Animation
Sprite sheets pack multiple animation frames into one image. You draw only the current frame's region each update. This is far more efficient than loading separate images.

blocks.output: Character animates through 8 frames at 12 FPS from a sprite sheet

blocks.value: Particle Systems
Particles are small, short-lived objects that create effects like explosions, fire, smoke, and magic. A particle system manages hundreds of particles efficiently.

blocks.output: Colorful explosion particles that fade out over time

blocks.question: What does lerp(10, 20, 0.5) return?
blocks.explanation: lerp(10, 20, 0.5) returns the midpoint: 10 + (20-10) * 0.5 = 15. At t=0 it returns start, at t=1 it returns end.

blocks.question: Why use sprite sheets instead of individual image files?
options: Fewer HTTP requests and better memory efficiency
blocks.correctAnswer: Fewer HTTP requests and better memory efficiency
blocks.explanation: Sprite sheets reduce network requests (one file vs many) and allow GPU batch rendering. They're the industry standard for 2D games.

blocks.question: Which Canvas property controls transparency when drawing?
blocks.explanation: ctx.globalAlpha sets the alpha (opacity) for all subsequent drawing operations, from 0 (fully transparent) to 1 (fully opaque).

blocks.value: Detecting Object Intersections

Collision detection determines when game objects touch or overlap. It's essential for gameplay: hitting enemies, collecting items, landing on platforms, and triggering events. We'll cover AABB (axis-aligned bounding boxes), circle collision, and pixel-perfect detection.

blocks.alt: Diagrams showing AABB, circle, and pixel-perfect collision types with hitboxes highlighted
blocks.caption: Different collision shapes for different accuracy needs

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Three-panel Comparison — Panel 1: 'AABB' — two rectangles with red overlap area. Panel 2: 'Circle' — two circles with distance line and overlap. Panel 3: 'Pixel-Perfect' — two irregular sprites with only actual opaque pixels checked. Label accuracy vs performance tradeoff below each.
AABB: Axis-Aligned Bounding Box
The fastest collision check. Works for rectangles that don't rotate. Check if the boxes overlap on both X and Y axes.

blocks.output: True when rectangles overlap, false when separated

blocks.value: Circle Collision
Perfect for circular objects like balls, bullets, and explosion radii. Calculate the distance between centers and compare to the sum of radii.

blocks.output: Accurate collision between circles and between circles and rectangles

blocks.value: Collision Response: Bouncing and Separation
Detecting collision is half the battle. You also need to respond: bounce objects apart, reduce health, play sounds, or trigger events. For simple bouncing, reverse velocity on the collision axis.

blocks.output: Ball correctly bounces off paddle with proper side detection

blocks.value: Spatial Partitioning: Grid-Based Collision
Checking every object against every other object is O(n²) — too slow for hundreds of objects. Divide space into a grid and only check objects in the same cell.

blocks.alt: Grid overlay on game world showing objects sorted into cells, only same-cell objects checked for collision
blocks.caption: Spatial hashing reduces collision checks from O(n²) to near O(n)

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Diagram — Game world divided into a 4x4 grid. Objects (circles) shown in different cells. Red arrows connect objects within the same cell for collision checking. Blue X marks show pairs in different cells that are NOT checked. Include formula: checks ≈ n × average objects per cell.

blocks.output: Efficient collision detection for hundreds of objects

blocks.question: What does AABB stand for?
blocks.explanation: AABB means the box edges are aligned with the X and Y axes (not rotated). It's the fastest collision check but only works for non-rotated rectangles.

blocks.question: Why avoid Math.sqrt() in circle collision when possible?
options: It's computationally expensive compared to comparing squared distances
It doesn't work with negative numbers
blocks.correctAnswer: It's computationally expensive compared to comparing squared distances
blocks.explanation: Math.sqrt() is slow. Instead of sqrt(dx² + dy²) < r1 + r2, compare dx² + dy² < (r1 + r2)² — same result, much faster.

blocks.question: Which spatial partitioning technique divides the world into uniform cells?
blocks.explanation: A spatial grid (or uniform grid) divides space into equal-sized cells. Objects only check collision with others in the same cell, reducing checks from O(n²) to near O(n).

blocks.value: Bringing Images into Your Game

Games need images — player characters, enemies, backgrounds, UI elements. Loading images asynchronously, managing an asset pipeline, and rendering them efficiently are critical skills. We'll build a robust asset manager that handles loading states and error recovery.

blocks.alt: Asset pipeline showing image files loading into an AssetManager, then being drawn by game objects
blocks.caption: The asset pipeline: load → cache → draw

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Pipeline Diagram — Left: Image files (PNG icons) flowing into a box labeled 'AssetManager' with a loading bar. Center: 'Cache' (storage box with image thumbnails). Right: Game objects pulling from cache to draw on Canvas. Arrow labeled 'drawImage()'. Include error handling path (red arrow) for failed loads.
The Asset Manager
A centralized system loads all game assets and tracks loading progress. It prevents duplicate loads, handles errors gracefully, and provides a clean API for the rest of your game.

blocks.output: All images loaded and cached, ready for rendering

blocks.value: Loading Screen with Progress Bar
Show players a progress bar while assets load. This prevents a blank screen and gives feedback on slow connections.

blocks.output: Animated loading screen with red progress bar filling to 100%

blocks.value: Sprite Rendering and Optimization
drawImage() has three forms: full image, sliced region (for sprite sheets), and scaled. Use the sliced version for animations and the scaled version for resolution independence.

blocks.output: Efficient sprite rendering with sprite sheet slicing and offscreen caching

blocks.value: 9-Slice Scaling for UI
UI elements like buttons and panels need to stretch without distorting corners. 9-slice scaling divides an image into 9 regions and scales only the center edges.

blocks.alt: 9-slice grid showing corner, edge, and center regions of a UI panel, with stretched version beside it
blocks.caption: 9-slice scaling preserves corners while stretching edges and center

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Diagram — Left: Original UI panel image with 3x3 grid overlay showing 9 regions (4 corners, 4 edges, 1 center). Right: Same panel stretched wider, with corners unchanged but edges and center stretched. Arrows show which regions scale horizontally/vertically/both. Label 'Corners: fixed', 'Edges: stretch 1 axis', 'Center: stretch both'.

blocks.output: UI panel stretched to any size while preserving corner details

blocks.question: Why use an offscreen canvas for static backgrounds?
options: It makes the image higher quality
It reduces draw calls by caching the composed result
It's required by the Canvas API
blocks.correctAnswer: It reduces draw calls by caching the composed result
blocks.explanation: Drawing complex backgrounds every frame is expensive. Render once to an offscreen canvas, then draw that single cached image each frame — much faster.

blocks.question: How many arguments does the full drawImage() method accept for sprite sheets?
blocks.explanation: The sliced version takes 9 arguments: image, sx, sy, sWidth, sHeight, dx, dy, dWidth, dHeight. This lets you draw a portion of a larger image (like a sprite sheet frame).

blocks.question: Which HTML element is created to load an image in JavaScript?
blocks.explanation: new Image() creates an HTMLImageElement. Set its src property to start loading, then use it with ctx.drawImage() once the onload event fires.

blocks.value: Building Your First Complete Game

Pong is the 'Hello, World' of game development. It teaches the core architecture you'll use in every game: Game class, Entity system, State management, and the render-update loop. We'll build it with clean OOP design that scales to larger projects.

blocks.alt: Class diagram showing Game, Ball, Paddle, InputManager, and CollisionSystem relationships
blocks.caption: Pong's architecture: modular classes with single responsibilities

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: UML Class Diagram — Boxes for Game, Ball, Paddle, InputManager, ScoreBoard. Arrows show relationships: Game 'has a' Ball, Game 'has a' Paddle (x2), Game 'uses' InputManager. Each box shows key methods. Use standard UML notation with clean lines. Color-code by responsibility type.
Architecture Overview

Our Pong architecture uses these principles:
• **Single Responsibility** — each class does one thing
• **Composition over Inheritance** — Game contains entities, doesn't extend them
• **Separation of Concerns** — rendering, physics, and input are separate
• **State Machine** — game has Menu, Playing, Paused, GameOver states

blocks.output: Complete Pong game architecture with state management and subsystems

blocks.value: The Ball Class
The ball handles its own movement, collision with walls, and reset logic. It uses delta time for consistent speed and emits particles on paddle hits.

blocks.output: Ball with motion trail, wall bouncing, and glow effects

blocks.value: The Paddle Class
Paddles handle player input (WASD/Arrows) and AI movement. The AI uses prediction to track the ball with adjustable difficulty.

blocks.output: Player-controlled and AI paddles with visual polish and smart AI behavior

blocks.value: Collision and Scoring System
The Game class ties everything together with collision detection, scoring logic, and particle effects on hits.

blocks.output: Responsive paddle hits with spin physics, speed ramping, and particle effects

blocks.value: Complete Project Structure
Your Pong project should be organized like this. This structure scales to much larger games.

📁 pong/
├── 📄 index.html
├── 📄 styles.css
├── 📁 js/
│   ├── 📄 main.js          // Entry point
│   ├── 📄 Game.js          // Main game class
│   ├── 📄 Ball.js          // Ball entity
│   ├── 📄 Paddle.js        // Paddle entity
│   ├── 📄 ScoreBoard.js    // Score display
│   ├── 📄 InputManager.js  // Keyboard input
│   ├── 📄 ParticleSystem.js // Visual effects
│   └── 📁 utils/
│       └── 📄 math.js      // lerp, clamp, etc.
└── 📁 assets/
    └── 📄 hit.wav          // Sound effect
blocks.output: Clean, scalable project structure for Pong and future games

blocks.value: What You Learned from Pong

• **Game Loop Architecture** — update/draw separation with delta time
• **Entity System** — self-contained objects with update() and draw()
• **Collision Detection** — AABB for paddles, circle-rect for ball
• **AI Behavior** — simple prediction-based opponent
• **Visual Polish** — particles, glow effects, motion trails
• **State Management** — menu, playing, paused, gameover states
• **Code Organization** — modular files with single responsibilities

blocks.question: Why cap delta time at 0.1 seconds in the game loop?
options: To limit the frame rate to 10 FPS
To prevent physics explosions when the tab loses focus
To make the game run slower
blocks.correctAnswer: To prevent physics explosions when the tab loses focus
blocks.explanation: If the tab is inactive, requestAnimationFrame pauses. When returning, dt could be several seconds. Capping dt prevents objects from teleporting through walls.

blocks.question: What design pattern does the Game class use to manage Ball and Paddle?
blocks.explanation: The Game class 'has a' Ball and 'has a' Paddle (composition), rather than 'is a' Ball (inheritance). This is more flexible and follows the 'favor composition over inheritance' principle.

blocks.question: Which method should you call to reverse a number's sign in JavaScript?
blocks.explanation: Math.sign(x) returns 1, -1, or 0 based on the sign of x. Combined with multiplication, it ensures a value moves in a specific direction: y += Math.sign(diff) * speed * dt.

blocks.value: Sound Makes Games Come Alive

Audio is half the gaming experience. The Web Audio API provides low-level sound synthesis, while the HTML5 Audio element handles simple playback. We'll build a hybrid audio manager that handles music, sound effects, spatial audio, and dynamic mixing.

blocks.alt: Audio pipeline showing sound files flowing through AudioManager with volume, pan, and effects controls to speakers
blocks.caption: The audio pipeline: load, process, mix, and play

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Pipeline Diagram — Left: Sound files (WAV/MP3 icons). Center: 'AudioManager' box with knobs for 'Master Volume', 'Music Volume', 'SFX Volume', 'Mute'. Right: Speaker icon with sound waves. Include a small 'Web Audio API' label and 'HTML5 Audio' fallback path. Use audio-themed colors (purple, cyan).
The Web Audio API

The Web Audio API is powerful but complex. It uses a node-based graph: source nodes (sound files) connect to effect nodes (volume, pan, reverb) which connect to the destination (speakers). This enables real-time audio manipulation.

blocks.output: Low-latency audio playback with volume, panning, and channel separation

blocks.value: Sound Manager for Games
A game-friendly wrapper around the Web Audio API. Preload sounds, play one-shots, loop music, and crossfade between tracks.

blocks.output: Game-ready sound manager with music crossfading and volume controls

blocks.value: Procedural Sound Effects
Generate sounds programmatically for small file sizes and infinite variation. Perfect for retro-style games where you want 8-bit beeps and boops without audio files.

blocks.output: Retro 8-bit jump, laser, and explosion sounds generated in real-time

blocks.value: Spatial Audio for Immersion
Pan sounds left/right based on their screen position. Explosions on the left should sound from the left speaker. This adds depth to 2D games.

blocks.output: Sounds positioned in stereo field based on in-game location

blocks.question: Why must AudioContext be resumed after a user interaction?
options: It's a bug in the API
Browsers block audio autoplay until user gesture
The context uses too much CPU when idle
It's required for mobile devices only
blocks.correctAnswer: Browsers block audio autoplay until user gesture
blocks.explanation: Modern browsers suspend AudioContext until a user interaction (click, keypress) to prevent annoying autoplay. You must call resume() after the first interaction.

blocks.question: Which Web Audio node controls left/right balance?
blocks.explanation: StereoPannerNode has a .pan property (-1 = full left, 1 = full right, 0 = center). PannerNode is for 3D spatial audio (more complex).

blocks.question: Which oscillator type produces a square wave for retro sounds?
blocks.explanation: oscillator.type = 'square' creates the harsh, buzzy sound characteristic of 8-bit and chiptune music. Other types: sine (smooth), sawtooth (brassy), triangle (mellow).

blocks.value: Realistic Movement and Forces

Game physics doesn't need to be scientifically perfect — it needs to feel good. We'll cover velocity, acceleration, gravity, friction, and impulse forces. These fundamentals power platformers, racing games, and physics puzzles.

blocks.alt: Diagram showing forces acting on a game object: gravity pulling down, velocity arrow, friction opposing motion
blocks.caption: Forces combine to create realistic game movement

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Physics Diagram — A game character (simple sprite) with labeled force vectors: red arrow down labeled 'gravity', green arrow right labeled 'velocity', orange arrow left labeled 'friction', blue arrow up labeled 'jump impulse'. Show the resultant motion vector as a dashed purple arrow. Include equations: v = v + a*dt, p = p + v*dt.
Velocity and Acceleration

Position changes by velocity. Velocity changes by acceleration. This is Euler integration — simple and sufficient for most games. Update velocity first, then position (semi-implicit Euler for stability).

blocks.output: Physics body with gravity, friction, forces, and jumping

blocks.value: Platformer Physics: Ground Detection
Ground detection prevents infinite jumping and enables variable jump height. Use raycasting downward or check collision with floor objects.

blocks.output: Platformer with variable jump height, ground detection, and platform collision

blocks.value: Verlet Integration for Ropes and Cloth
Verlet integration is perfect for soft body physics: ropes, cloth, hair, and chains. It stores positions instead of velocities, making constraints (like fixed lengths) easy to enforce.

blocks.output: Physics-based rope simulation with realistic swinging and gravity

blocks.value: Collision Resolution: Penetration Correction
When objects overlap, push them apart so they don't get stuck. Calculate penetration depth and move objects along the collision normal.

blocks.output: Objects correctly separate and bounce after collision

blocks.question: Why use semi-implicit Euler (velocity then position) instead of explicit Euler?
options: It's required by the Canvas API
blocks.explanation: Semi-implicit Euler updates velocity before position. This makes it more stable (less likely to explode) and better at conserving energy compared to explicit Euler which can gain energy over time.

blocks.question: What does Verlet integration store instead of velocity?
blocks.explanation: Verlet stores current position and previous position. Velocity is derived from the difference between them. This makes constraints (like fixed rope lengths) trivial to enforce.

blocks.question: Which force constantly pulls objects downward in most games?
blocks.explanation: Gravity is the constant downward acceleration (typically 800-1500 px/s² in 2D games). It's applied every frame to create falling, jumping arcs, and grounded movement.

blocks.value: Building Worlds with Tiles

Tilemaps are the backbone of 2D level design. They store level data in grids (arrays) and render only visible tiles for performance. We'll cover orthogonal (top-down/side-view) tilemaps, tilesets, collision layers, and level editors.

blocks.alt: Tilemap showing 32x32 pixel tiles forming a game level with ground, walls, and decorations
blocks.caption: A tilemap: small reusable tiles combined into large, complex levels

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Diagram — Left: Tileset image showing a 4x4 grid of 32x32 tiles (grass, dirt, wall, water, etc.) with numbers 0-15. Right: A level built from those tiles showing a platformer scene. Arrows connect tile numbers to their placements. Include a zoomed-in view showing the grid overlay. Use pixel-art style for tiles.
Tilemap Data Structure
Store levels as 2D arrays where each number represents a tile ID. Multiple layers allow foreground, background, and collision data.

blocks.output: Tilemap system with multi-layer support and collision queries

blocks.value: Rendering Only Visible Tiles
Don't draw tiles outside the camera view! Calculate the visible tile range and only render those. This keeps huge levels running at 60 FPS.

blocks.output: Only visible tiles rendered, maintaining 60 FPS on large maps

blocks.value: Loading Tiled Editor Maps
Tiled is the industry-standard level editor. It exports JSON files that your game can load directly. Parse layer data, tilesets, and object layers for spawn points and triggers.

blocks.output: Tiled editor levels loaded and parsed into game-ready format

blocks.value: Autotiling: Smart Tile Placement
Autotiling automatically selects the correct tile variant based on neighboring tiles. A wall tile becomes a corner, edge, or center piece depending on what's around it.

blocks.alt: Grid showing how autotiling selects different wall tiles based on neighbor configuration using bitmasking
blocks.caption: Autotiling uses neighbor bitmasking to select the correct tile variant

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Diagram — 3x3 grid of tile configurations. Each cell shows a different wall tile (corner, edge, center, etc.) with small neighbor indicators (N, S, E, W). Below: the bitmask formula: value = N*1 + W*2 + E*4 + S*8. Show example: N+W neighbors = value 3 = top-left corner tile. Use grid with arrows.

blocks.output: Seamless terrain with correct edge and corner tiles

blocks.question: Why only render visible tiles instead of the entire map?
options: It dramatically improves performance on large maps
It's required by the Canvas API
blocks.correctAnswer: It dramatically improves performance on large maps
blocks.explanation: Drawing thousands of off-screen tiles wastes GPU time. Culling to the camera viewport reduces draw calls from thousands to hundreds, maintaining 60 FPS.

blocks.question: What does Tiled export that your game can load directly?
options: JSON files with layer and tileset data
blocks.correctAnswer: JSON files with layer and tileset data
blocks.explanation: Tiled exports JSON containing map dimensions, layer data (as 1D arrays), tileset references, and object layers. Your game parses this to reconstruct the level.

blocks.question: What technique automatically selects tile variants based on neighbors?
blocks.explanation: Autotiling (or auto-tiling) uses neighbor information to select the correct tile graphic. Common methods are 4-bit (16 tiles) and 8-bit (48 tiles) bitmasking.

blocks.value: Cinematography in 2D Games

A great camera system is invisible — players never think about it, but they feel it. We'll build cameras that follow smoothly, shake on impacts, zoom dynamically, and confine to level bounds. Good camera work transforms good games into great ones.

blocks.alt: Comparison showing rigid camera vs smooth camera with deadzone, and camera with screen shake effect
blocks.caption: Camera behavior dramatically changes how a game feels

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Three-panel Comparison — Panel 1: 'Rigid' — camera locked to player, jerky movement shown with red jagged path. Panel 2: 'Smooth + Deadzone' — camera lags slightly, smooth curved path, deadzone box around player. Panel 3: 'With Shake' — same as panel 2 but with vibration effect on impact. Use motion lines to show camera movement.
Smooth Follow with Deadzone
A deadzone is an area where the camera doesn't move. The player can move within this zone without shifting the view. Only when they exit the deadzone does the camera smoothly catch up.

blocks.output: Camera smoothly follows player with configurable deadzone and bounds

blocks.value: Screen Shake

Screen shake adds impact to explosions, heavy landings, and damage. Use random offsets that decay over time. Trauma-based systems (inspired by Squirrel Eiserloh's GDC talk) produce more natural shake.

blocks.output: Impactful screen shake with trauma-based intensity and smooth decay

blocks.value: Camera Zoom and Panning
Zoom in for precision platforming, zoom out for exploration. Smooth zoom transitions prevent disorientation. Pan to highlight points of interest.

blocks.output: Smooth zooming camera with bounds and fit-to-content modes

blocks.value: Multi-Target Camera
In multiplayer or games with multiple important objects, the camera should frame all targets. Calculate the bounding box of all targets and center/zoom to fit.

blocks.output: Camera automatically frames all players with smooth transitions

blocks.question: What is a camera deadzone?
options: An area where the game doesn't render
A region where the camera doesn't move even if the player does
A place where enemies can't spawn
blocks.correctAnswer: A region where the camera doesn't move even if the player does
blocks.explanation: A deadzone is a rectangular area around the screen center. The player can move within it without the camera following, reducing motion sickness and creating a more stable view.

blocks.question: Why square the trauma value in screen shake calculations?
options: To create non-linear falloff (strong initial shake, gentle fade)
blocks.correctAnswer: To create non-linear falloff (strong initial shake, gentle fade)
blocks.explanation: Squaring trauma (shake = trauma²) creates a non-linear curve. High trauma produces strong shake, but as trauma decreases, the shake falls off faster, feeling more natural than linear decay.

blocks.question: Which Canvas method saves the current transform state before camera application?
blocks.explanation: ctx.save() pushes the current state (transforms, styles, clipping) onto a stack. After drawing the world, ctx.restore() pops it back, ensuring UI draws in screen space without camera transforms.

blocks.value: Game States and Persistence
Clean state transitions with localStorage for high scores. The menu shows the bird idle, playing adds physics, and gameover shows the final score with a medal.

blocks.output: Polished game over screen with score board, medal system, and restart prompt

blocks.value: What You Learned from Flappy Bird

• **Object Pooling** — recycle entities instead of garbage collecting
• **Procedural Generation** — infinite content with controlled randomness
• **Mobile Input** — touch events with preventDefault for responsive controls
• **Screen Shake** — trauma-based camera effects for impact
• **Persistence** — localStorage for high scores and settings
• **Game Feel** — forgiving hitboxes, smooth animations, visual polish
• **Parallax Scrolling** — multiple background layers at different speeds

blocks.question: What is the main benefit of object pooling in Flappy Bird?
blocks.explanation: Creating and destroying objects constantly triggers JavaScript's garbage collector, causing frame drops. Object pooling reuses a fixed set of objects, maintaining consistent 60 FPS.

blocks.question: Why use preventDefault() on touch events?
options: To stop the browser from scrolling/zooming the page
It's required by the Canvas API
blocks.correctAnswer: To stop the browser from scrolling/zooming the page
blocks.explanation: Browsers default to scrolling on touch. preventDefault() stops this behavior so your game receives the touch as input instead of the browser treating it as a page scroll gesture.

blocks.question: Which Web Storage API saves data persistently in the browser?
blocks.explanation: localStorage stores key-value pairs persistently (until explicitly cleared). Unlike sessionStorage, it survives page reloads and browser restarts. Perfect for high scores and settings.

blocks.value: Managing Complex Game Flow

As games grow, hardcoded if/else state logic becomes unmaintainable. A State Machine (or State Pattern) cleanly separates each game state into its own class with enter, update, draw, and exit methods. This scales from simple menus to complex RPG dialogue systems.

blocks.alt: State machine diagram showing MenuState, PlayState, PauseState, GameOverState with transition arrows
blocks.caption: Each state is isolated — transitions happen through a central manager

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: State Machine Diagram — Circles for states: Menu (green), Playing (blue), Paused (yellow), GameOver (red). Arrows show transitions: Menu→Playing (start), Playing→Paused (esc), Paused→Playing (resume), Playing→GameOver (die), GameOver→Menu (restart). Use standard state machine notation with labeled transitions.
The State Pattern

Each state is a class implementing a common interface. The Game class holds a reference to the current state and delegates update/draw/input to it. States can transition to other states by returning the next state from update().

blocks.output: Clean state machine with registered states and automatic transitions

blocks.value: Concrete State Implementations
Each state handles its own logic. The Playing state runs the game, PauseState freezes and shows a menu, GameOverState displays final stats.

blocks.output: Menu, Playing, and Pause states with clean transitions and isolated logic

blocks.value: Hierarchical State Machines
Complex games need substates. A Player state machine can have Grounded, Jumping, Falling, and Attacking states, each with their own physics and animations.

blocks.output: Player behavior cleanly separated into grounded, jumping, and falling states

blocks.question: What is the main advantage of the State Pattern over if/else state logic?
options: It isolates state logic into separate, testable classes
blocks.correctAnswer: It isolates state logic into separate, testable classes
blocks.explanation: The State Pattern puts each state's behavior in its own class. This prevents giant switch statements, makes states reusable, and allows easy addition of new states without modifying existing code.

blocks.question: What methods does each state typically implement?
blocks.explanation: Game states typically have enter() (setup), update() (logic), draw() (rendering), and exit() (cleanup). This lifecycle ensures clean transitions and resource management.

blocks.question: Which design principle does the State Pattern follow?
blocks.explanation: The State Pattern follows the Open/Closed Principle: open for extension (add new states), closed for modification (existing states don't change). It also follows Single Responsibility by isolating each state's behavior.

blocks.value: Data-Oriented Game Architecture

ECS is the architecture powering most modern game engines (Unity, Unreal). Instead of inheritance hierarchies, you compose entities from components and process them with systems. This is more flexible, cache-friendly, and scales to thousands of entities.

blocks.alt: Diagram showing Entity as container, Components as data (Position, Velocity, Sprite), Systems as processors (Movement, Render, Collision)
blocks.caption: ECS: Entities are IDs, Components are data, Systems are logic

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Architecture Diagram — Top: 'Entity' (just an ID number). Middle: Three boxes labeled 'Components' — Position {x,y}, Velocity {vx,vy}, Sprite {image, frame}. Bottom: Three boxes labeled 'Systems' — MovementSystem (arrow to Position+Velocity), RenderSystem (arrow to Position+Sprite), CollisionSystem (arrow to Position). Show entity 42 connected to all three components. Use clean, modern diagram style.
Core ECS Implementation
An entity is just a unique number. Components are plain data objects stored in arrays. Systems iterate over entities that have the required components and update them.

blocks.output: Core ECS world with entity creation, component storage, and system execution

blocks.value: Components: Pure Data
Components contain no logic — only data. This makes them trivial to serialize (save/load) and network (multiplayer).

blocks.output: Player and enemy entities composed from reusable data components

blocks.value: Systems: The Logic Processors
Systems query entities with specific components and update them. MovementSystem needs Position + Velocity. RenderSystem needs Position + Sprite. This is where all game logic lives.

blocks.output: Movement, render, and collision systems processing entity components

blocks.value: When to Use ECS vs OOP

ECS shines when you have many entities with mixed behaviors. For small games, OOP (classes with inheritance) is simpler. Use ECS when:
• You have 100+ entities
• Entity behaviors combine in many ways
• You need save/load serialization
• You're building an engine, not just a game

blocks.question: What does an Entity represent in ECS?
blocks.explanation: In ECS, an entity is purely an ID number. It has no data or behavior of its own. All data lives in components, and all behavior lives in systems.

blocks.question: Which ECS element contains game logic?
blocks.explanation: Systems contain all logic. They query entities with specific components and update them. Components are pure data with no methods, and entities are just IDs.

blocks.question: What data structure typically stores components in ECS?
blocks.explanation: Components are stored in Maps (or arrays) keyed by entity ID. This allows O(1) lookup of any component for any entity. world.components.get('position').get(entityId) retrieves a specific entity's position.

blocks.value: Bringing Enemies to Life

Game AI doesn't need to be intelligent — it needs to be fun. We'll cover finite state machines for enemy behavior, A* pathfinding for navigation, and steering behaviors for natural movement. These tools create enemies that feel challenging but fair.

blocks.alt: Diagram showing enemy AI states: Patrol, Chase, Attack, Flee with transition conditions
blocks.caption: Enemy AI uses states and sensors to decide behavior

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: AI State Diagram — Enemy sprite in center with four states around it: Patrol (walking), Chase (running), Attack (sword), Flee (running away). Arrows with conditions: 'player in range' (Patrol→Chase), 'player close' (Chase→Attack), 'health < 20%' (Attack→Flee), 'player far' (any→Patrol). Use game-themed icons for each state.
Finite State Machine AI
Enemies cycle through states based on conditions. A guard patrols until seeing the player, then chases, attacks when close, and flees when low on health.

blocks.output: Enemy AI with patrol, chase, attack, and flee behaviors

blocks.value: A* Pathfinding
A* (A-Star) finds the shortest path around obstacles. It combines the cost to reach a node (Dijkstra) with an estimate to the goal (heuristic) for efficient exploration.

blocks.output: Shortest path around obstacles from start to goal

blocks.value: Steering Behaviors
Steering behaviors create natural, fluid movement. Combine seek, flee, arrive, wander, and separation for complex emergent behaviors like flocking and swarming.

blocks.output: Natural steering forces for seek, flee, wander, and separation behaviors

blocks.value: Combining Behaviors: Flocking
Flocking (boids) emerges from three simple rules: separation (don't crowd), alignment (match velocity), and cohesion (stay with group). Weight and combine these forces.

blocks.output: Emergent flocking behavior with separation, alignment, and cohesion

blocks.question: What makes A* more efficient than Dijkstra's algorithm?
options: It uses a heuristic to guide search toward the goal
blocks.correctAnswer: It uses a heuristic to guide search toward the goal
blocks.explanation: A* combines actual cost from start (g) with estimated cost to goal (h). This heuristic guides the search toward the target, exploring far fewer nodes than Dijkstra which explores equally in all directions.

blocks.question: Which steering behavior makes agents avoid crowding each other?
blocks.explanation: Separation steers agents away from nearby neighbors. Combined with alignment (match direction) and cohesion (move toward center), it creates realistic flocking behavior.

blocks.question: What is the common name for Craig Reynolds' flocking algorithm?
blocks.explanation: Boids (short for 'bird-oid objects') is Craig Reynolds' 1986 flocking algorithm. It demonstrates emergent behavior from three simple rules: separation, alignment, and cohesion.

blocks.value: Building Game Interfaces

Game UI includes HUDs (heads-up displays), menus, dialogs, and tooltips. Unlike web UI, game UI renders on Canvas and must update every frame. We'll build a UI system with buttons, sliders, progress bars, and text rendering that feels responsive and polished.

blocks.alt: Game UI showing health bar, ammo counter, minimap, and interactive buttons all rendered on Canvas
blocks.caption: A complete game UI rendered entirely on Canvas

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: UI Mockup — Canvas with game scene in background. Overlay elements: top-left health bar (green fill, red background), top-right ammo '30/90', bottom-center ability icons with cooldown overlays, bottom-left minimap, center 'LEVEL UP!' text with glow. Show hover state on one button (brighter). Use game UI aesthetic (dark panels, bright accents).
UI Element Base Class
All UI elements share position, size, visibility, and event handling. A base class provides this foundation; specific elements override draw() and handleInput().

blocks.output: Base UI element with hierarchy, hit detection, and event bubbling

blocks.value: Button, Slider, and Progress Bar
Common UI widgets built on the base class. Buttons have hover/pressed states. Sliders handle drag input. Progress bars animate smoothly.

blocks.output: Interactive button, animated health bar, and draggable slider widgets

blocks.value: Canvas Text Rendering with Word Wrap
Canvas text doesn't word-wrap automatically. Build a text renderer that handles wrapping, alignment, and shadow effects for dialogs and descriptions.

blocks.output: Word-wrapped text and shadow effects for readable game UI

blocks.value: Tooltip System
Tooltips appear on hover, showing item stats or ability descriptions. Position them intelligently to avoid going off-screen.

blocks.output: Smart tooltips that reposition to stay on screen

blocks.question: Why build UI on Canvas instead of using HTML/CSS DOM elements?
options: For pixel-perfect control, game-themed styling, and unified rendering
DOM elements don't work with games
It's required by the Canvas API
blocks.correctAnswer: For pixel-perfect control, game-themed styling, and unified rendering
blocks.explanation: While DOM UI is easier, Canvas UI gives pixel-perfect control over every pixel, consistent game-themed styling, and unified rendering (no DOM/Canvas layering issues). It's essential for full-screen immersive games.

blocks.question: What technique makes health bars animate smoothly when taking damage?
options: Lerp between current and target values each frame
blocks.correctAnswer: Lerp between current and target values each frame
blocks.explanation: Smooth health bars store a 'display value' that lerps toward the actual health value each frame: displayValue += (target - display) * speed * dt. This creates a satisfying visual delay.

blocks.question: Which Canvas property adds a shadow behind drawn text and shapes?
blocks.explanation: ctx.shadowBlur, shadowColor, shadowOffsetX, and shadowOffsetY create drop shadows. Set shadowBlur > 0 and shadowColor to enable the effect. Remember to save/restore or reset to 0 when done.
